source.title: CLaM-TTS: Improving Neural Codec Language Model for Zero-Shot Text-to-Speech
source.authors: Jaehyeon Kim; Ke-On Lee; Seung-Jun Chung; Jaewoong Cho

record.tranche_reason: Tests the data-scale-to-task-performance part of V6 using TTS evaluation metrics rather than held-out language-model loss; it does not measure a loss scaling law.
record.gate_note: The study compares three training-data volumes for ByT5-base TTS models and reports WER, CER, and speaker similarity, so those outcomes bear on V6. It does not report held-out pretraining loss, parameter/token/compute sweeps, extrapolation, or a compute-optimal allocation. The T5-variant comparisons in Appendix D.2 vary pretraining/input variants rather than scale or measured pretraining loss, so they are not extracted as scaling results.
record.test_reason: This is a zero-shot TTS method paper. Its only scale-related result is a three-point ablation (Appendix D.4, Table 14) over TTS training-data volume (22K/44K/55K hours) for a ByT5-base text-to-code model, scored by WER, CER and SIM-o. It fits no power law and makes no prediction or extrapolation. The varied data is the task's own training data, not pretraining, and the 55K set also changes data composition (adds GigaSpeech, LibriTTS-R, VCTK, LJSpeech). Three monotone-ish points cannot show power-law form (V1/V5) or predictability with scale or pretraining loss (V6). Kaplan et al. is cited only in the introduction, so the study neither tests nor relies on the scaling-law claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors say performance improves with more training data: small data degrades all metrics, and the large set improves SIM-o while maintaining WER/CER. They state this "strongly indicates" scaling data boosts performance. They fit no law and make no claim about pretraining-loss scaling.
record.recipe_differences: Compares training-data volumes and downstream TTS metrics, not held-out language-model loss or parameter/token/compute scaling; no power-law fitting or compute-optimal allocation.
record.method_sensitivity: Training-data volume changes CER and SIM-o, while WER improves from 22K to 44K hours and then plateaus at 55K hours.

fits_no_version.finding: TTS task metrics (CER, SIM-o, and WER up to 44K) improve as TTS training data grows from 22K to 55K hours for a ByT5-base text-to-code model. WER plateaus at 55K, and the largest set also changes data domains.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In codec-LM zero-shot TTS, more training data monotonically improves intelligibility/similarity metrics over a 2.5x range (no functional form tested).

record.problems: The data-scale comparison has only three training volumes and uses ByT5-base models; the table reports no uncertainty estimates. It measures downstream TTS metrics, not held-out pretraining loss, and provides no power-law fit.
record.rows_left_out: No results bearing on the tested V6 data-volume comparison were left out. Appendix D.2's T5-variant/input-format results are not extracted because they do not vary scale or measure pretraining loss.

untested.parts: No held-out pretraining loss and no parameter/token/compute sweep.
No shape comparison at fixed parameter count. The codeword-rate and T5-variant ablations vary other things.
The speech modality is present, but no power-law form is fitted for data or model scale.
There is no downstream-vs-scale or downstream-vs-pretraining-loss relation. The data-volume ablation is task training data with three points and no fit.

record.verdict_notes: Reader's V6 'tests' relation and its supports/limits_scope labels are removed. The rows measure a non-pretraining TTS training-data ablation with only three points. No uncertainty is reported, and scale is confounded with data composition at 55K, so no version's form or predictability can be assessed. The T5-variant ablation (Table 11) compares pretraining type, not scale, and is correctly excluded.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss or power-law fit over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fit or large-run loss prediction.
No fixed-compute allocation or parameter/token growth comparison.
No controlled comparison of architecture shape at fixed parameter count.
The study concerns speech generation, but does not test whether a power-law loss form holds in another modality or training regime.
Tests training-data volume against TTS task metrics for ByT5-base only; does not test performance against pretraining loss, other model scales, or a broad range of scales.
No comparison of fitted exponents, fitting choices, or curve departures from a power law.
